citation: crates/muster-core/src/typeable.rs, crates/muster-herdr/src/control_socket.rs, and kan card a_27Y4QtzyK. There is no oracle above these: how long a pane may render before Muster accuses its bridge is Muster's call, and these cases are where it is written down. The five seconds the seam actually uses is argued from tools/smoke-launch.py, which waits 2.0s after `app.ready` for a healthy bridge to start, dial back and paint.
why:
A pane becomes typeable when its bridge dials the socket Muster bound for it, and until then it renders, paints and discards every keystroke. Three separate bugs in this repo all ended in exactly that state - the bridge failed to dial, the socket path had moved, the channel could not be opened - and none of them said anything until somebody typed. Both ends of the wait are already known to the core, so the only thing missing was a deadline between them, which is what these cases pin.

Every case answers with the diff rather than the current set, because raising and clearing are the two things the caller can do, and getting the second one wrong is how a stale error outlives the pane it was about. `next_wake` is answered by every case too, because a loop around this has exactly two ways to go wrong: spinning on a pane it has already reported, and sleeping through one that fell overdue while it was busy elsewhere.

Times are nanoseconds, matching the monotonic clock the seam counts in. `raised` and `cleared` accumulate over every `reconcile` a case performs, so a case with two readings shows whether the second one had anything new to say. `next_wake` is asked once, at the case's `now` or at its last reading.

A wait starts either way a pane can be waiting: `opened` is a socket bound with no bridge yet, and `ended` is the same wait restarting after one stopped, carrying how it stopped. The second is why the sentence differs at all - a pane looks identical in every one of these cases and the thing to do differs in all of them, and until they were told apart every one of them read as `look in the run log`.

cases.name: a pane whose bridge never dials is reported once the deadline passes
cases.why: The base case, and the whole point: before this the same fact reached the run log and the window said nothing, so the first person to know was whoever typed into a pane that looked fine. The sentence is pinned here rather than in every case because it is one sentence - the deadline in it rather than the elapsed time, so that a condition which stays true has nothing new to say on the next reading.

expect.detail: The pane local/w1:p1 has had a socket open for over 5s, and nothing has dialed it - the bridge carrying this pane's keystrokes either never started or cannot reach the socket. Everything typed into this pane is discarded and it goes on rendering, so it looks frozen rather than broken; every other pane in the window is unaffected. The run log has the cause: look for `channel.accept.failed`, `bridge.exited.reported` and `pane.channel.unavailable`. Closing this pane and opening it again starts a new bridge.

cases.name: a pane whose terminal was taken says which window has it
cases.why: Nothing is broken here and the sentence must not read as though something is: another window asked for this pane and herdr gave it to them, which is the arrangement herdr allows. What the person needs is where their pane went and how to get it back, and neither is derivable from a blank pane.

expect.detail: Another client attached to the pane local/w1:p1 and took its terminal, so this window has stopped drawing it - most often a second Muster window that was opened onto the same machine. Only one client may hold a herdr terminal, so nothing here can show it while that one does; the agent itself is untouched and every other pane in this window is unaffected. Whichever window is showing it now is the one to type into. To bring it back here instead, close this pane and open it again - the fresh bridge takes the terminal the way that one did.

cases.name: a pane whose attach was refused names the client holding it
cases.why: The failure that cost a working day, and the one nobody guesses: a herdr client whose transport died goes on holding the terminal, so every attach after a relaunch is refused by a machine that is otherwise perfectly healthy. The pane read `Process exited. Press any key to close the terminal.` and the way out - kill three processes over ssh - was not derivable from anything on screen.

steps.reason: terminal attach failed: terminal term_65a6bff3dab3da already has an attached client; retry with --takeover

expect.detail: The pane devenv/w4:p2 has been dark for over 5s: something else is holding its terminal, and every bridge Muster started for it was refused. Only one client may hold a herdr terminal, and one whose connection died goes on holding it without noticing - most often a previous Muster's client, still on the far machine. The agent behind this pane is untouched and every other pane in the window is unaffected. `ssh <host> 'pkill -f "terminal session control w4:p2"'` releases it, and closing this pane and opening it again then starts a bridge that attaches.

cases.name: a pane whose connection went says which machine to check
cases.why: A dropped VPN, and the case that recovers on its own once the machine is reachable - so the sentence has to say that rather than send somebody looking for a fault. It also has to say the agent is untouched, because a pane frozen on its last frame reads as work lost.

steps.reason: herdr's stream ended without a closing frame

expect.detail: The pane devenv/w4:p1 lost the connection carrying it and has not got one back within 5s. It shows what it last painted and takes no keystrokes; the agent behind it is untouched, and panes on other machines in this window are unaffected. Check that the machine holding it is reachable - the run log says `tunnel.down` when the connection is the reason, and Muster keeps trying. Closing this pane and opening it again starts a fresh bridge.

cases.name: a pane still inside its deadline is not accused
cases.why: A bridge takes measurable time to start, dial and paint, and a window that reported every pane during its first moments would be a window nobody reads. The deadline separates slow from broken, so the boundary is exclusive on the near side - and one nanosecond short of it, the answer is to wait that nanosecond.

cases.name: the same overdue pane is not news on the second reading
cases.why: The watch runs on a clock, so it asks repeatedly about a condition that stays true. If every reading counted as news the roster would republish and reopen itself for as long as the pane stayed quiet - which is the nagging that keying a problem by its condition was meant to end.

cases.name: a bridge that dials in late takes the problem back
cases.why: A pane reported after five seconds whose bridge turns up at six is a working pane, and the box disappearing is the only confirmation anybody gets that it started working. Leaving it raised would teach whoever saw it to stop believing the roster.

cases.name: a pane closed while overdue takes its problem with it
cases.why: The case that goes wrong when it is forgotten. A pane that was deaf and is now gone would otherwise leave an error in the roster naming something nobody can look at, and no later event would ever clear it - the pane it was about is the thing that no longer exists.

cases.name: one deaf pane among working ones is reported precisely
cases.why: Fourteen panes working and one deaf is the case worth reporting exactly, and it is why the condition is keyed per pane rather than per window. A window-wide answer would either accuse the working panes or say nothing while one of them swallowed everything typed into it.

cases.name: two daemons handing out the same pane id are two panes
cases.why: Both daemons in a window call their first pane w1:p1, so anything keyed by pane alone lets one machine's pane answer for the other's. The key carries the daemon for the same reason every other cross-daemon key in the core does.

cases.name: a bridge that exited starts the wait again
cases.why: A pane keeps its channel while its surface is thrown away and built again, so the replacement bridge has to dial too. control_socket.rs names this as the reason its accept loop runs more than once, and a replacement that never arrives is the same deaf pane - so the clock restarts rather than the pane being considered settled for good.

cases.name: a deadline of zero watches nothing
cases.why: The honest answer for a run with no bridges to wait for, and what the seam's own knob means when it is set to 0. Off has to mean off rather than nearly-immediately: a zero read as a deadline that has always passed would accuse every pane the moment its socket was bound.

cases.name: nothing waiting means nothing to wake up for
cases.why: An idle window should cost no wakeups at all, which is what lets the watch be a parked thread rather than a tick. This is the answer that decides it.

cases.name: the wake is the earliest deadline among the panes waiting
cases.why: So that a caller holding a real clock sleeps exactly as long as it has to, rather than polling. The earliest, because a pane opened later must not push back the report of one opened earlier.

cases.name: a pane already reported does not decide when to wake next
cases.why: The first of two ways a loop around this misbehaves. Nothing further happens to a reported pane on the clock alone - only a bridge dialing in or the pane closing changes its answer, and both of those tell the caller directly - so counting it would answer zero forever and spin. What decides here is the pane still waiting behind it.

cases.name: an overdue pane nobody has reported yet wants waking immediately
cases.why: The other way it goes wrong. A pane that fell overdue while the caller was busy publishing something else must not be slept through, because on a quiet window nothing else would ever wake it - so the answer is zero rather than nothing, until it has actually been reported.
